options.text: A directional growth response toward or away from a stimulus
options.explanation: Tropisms are directional growth responses of plants.

options.text: A rapid movement of a whole plant
options.explanation: Plants respond by growth, not by moving their position.
Chemicals called auxins cause tropisms but are not tropisms themselves.
The named tropisms answer light and gravity.

questions.stem: How do shoots respond to light?

options.explanation: Phototropism is a core plant response.

options.text: Positive phototropism — growth toward the light
options.explanation: Shoots grow toward light to catch sunlight for leaves.

options.text: Negative phototropism — growth away from light
options.explanation: That describes roots' light response.
That is the roots' gravity response.

questions.stem: How do roots respond to gravity?

options.explanation: Phototropism answers light, not gravity.
Root growth is directional, not random.

options.text: Positive geotropism — growth toward gravity, into the soil
options.explanation: Roots grow downward with gravity to anchor and absorb water.

options.text: Negative geotropism — growth away from gravity
options.explanation: That is the shoots' gravity response.

questions.stem: Which pairing describes roots' response to light correctly?

options.explanation: The table assigns roots a negative phototropic response.

options.text: Roots bend toward light to photosynthesise
options.explanation: Photosynthesis is the shoots' job.
Roots grow away from light.

options.text: Negative phototropism — growth away from the light source
options.explanation: Roots grow downward into soil, away from light.

questions.stem: Why do roots grow downward into the soil?

options.text: To hold the plant firm and draw up soil water plus dissolved minerals
options.explanation: Those are the stated reasons for downward root growth.
Predator escape is not the named reason.
Reproduction is unrelated to root direction.
Light is the shoots' target.

questions.modelAnswer: A plant's directional growth response to gravity, toward it (positive, as in roots) or away (negative, as in shoots).

questions.stem: State the two tropism signs a shoot displays.
questions.modelAnswer: Positive phototropism toward light and negative geotropism away from gravity.

questions.stem: Explain why a shoot's positive phototropic response helps the plant survive.
questions.modelAnswer: Growing toward light positions the leaves where they can absorb the most sunlight for photosynthesis, so the plant makes more food, grows stronger and outcompetes shaded neighbours — the tropism converts a stimulus directly into a survival advantage.

questions.stem: A seedling germinates on a dark windowsill with light coming from one side only. Describe its expected growth pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The shoot curves toward the window (positive phototropism) while growing upward against gravity (negative geotropism); the root grows away from the light and downward into the compost with gravity (positive geotropism, negative phototropism).

options.explanation: Production is tied to shoot tips, not leaves or darkness.

options.text: In the tips of growing shoots
options.explanation: Auxin is mostly made in the shoot tips.
Root hairs absorb water; they do not make auxin here.
Flowers handle reproduction in this note's scope.

questions.stem: What does auxin do to cells behind the tip?

options.text: Kills them to shorten the shoot
options.explanation: Auxin promotes growth, not death.
No such transformation is described.
Auxin makes existing cells get longer; more auxin means faster elongation.

options.text: Causes them to divide into many new cells
options.explanation: The exam hint is explicit — auxin elongates existing cells, it does not multiply them.

questions.stem: Under one-sided light, where does auxin accumulate?

options.explanation: That would bend the shoot away from light — the opposite of what happens.
Even spreading happens under all-round light, not one-sided light.

options.text: It drains out of the roots
options.explanation: Auxin stays within the shoot's growing region.

options.text: On the shaded side of the shoot
options.explanation: Auxin concentrates on the side away from the light.

questions.stem: What is the result of the shaded side elongating faster?

options.text: The shoot bends and grows in the direction of the light
options.explanation: Faster shaded-side growth curves the shoot sunward.

options.text: The shoot bends away from the light
options.explanation: That would need the sunlit side to elongate faster.
Growth bending, not breaking, occurs.
Growth continues — unevenly.

questions.stem: Which statement about auxin and cell number is correct?

options.text: Auxin increases the number of cells in the shoot
options.explanation: This is precisely the trap — auxin does not increase cell number.

options.text: Auxin makes the cells that already exist get longer
options.explanation: Elongation of existing cells is the correct mechanism.
No cell removal is involved.

options.text: Cell number changes only in roots
options.explanation: The note concerns shoot elongation; cell number is unchanged.

questions.stem: State where auxin is made and where it acts.
questions.modelAnswer: Made in the shoot tips; it diffuses just behind the tip into the elongation zone.

questions.stem: Give the dose relationship between auxin and elongation.
questions.modelAnswer: The more auxin present, the faster the cells elongate and grow.

questions.stem: Explain why writing 'the shoot grows toward the light because cells divide' loses marks.
questions.modelAnswer: Because division implies new cells are being made, which is wrong: auxin causes the cells that already exist behind the tip to elongate, so the shoot bends by existing cells getting longer — claiming division shows the mechanism has been misidentified.

questions.stem: A potted plant sits in a room whose only window is to its left. Using auxin, explain the shape it develops after two weeks.
questions.modelAnswer: Light from the left makes auxin accumulate on the right (shaded) side of the shoot; those cells elongate faster than the lit side, so the stem curves leftward toward the window — a visible positive phototropic bend.
